To disentangle the contribution of agentic scaffolding from the underlying LLM's intrinsic behavior on the same inputs, we compared outcomes between the full agent setting and a non-agent baseline across all profiles except homonymous profiles (category 4), using Gemini 3 Pro as a representative model. For the non-agent setting, we provided the complete patient profile in dictionary format directly in the prompt and asked the model to make a submission or withholding decision (Supplementary Prompt 4) without any additional workflow scaffolding. A preliminary manual review of a subset of responses revealed two patterns not observed in the agentic setting: 1) the model flagged inherent characteristics of the synthetic data in both compliant and deficient profiles, such as provider National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers deviating from real-world formatting conventions and addresses not matching known geographic entries; 2) the model often reported both designed and nondesigned issues for the same deficient profile, so that correct withholding and error misattribution applied simultaneously. We therefore used a modified classifier prompt that allowed both labels (Supplementary Prompt 5). Figure 4(c) shows that the model withheld 100.0% of the profiles regardless of the compliance status and correctly identified the designed issue in 91.3% of deficient profiles; 62.3% of these outputs with correct identifications also cited alongside at least one other non-designed issue. Out of all deficient profiles, synthetic-data related artifacts were cited in 29.7% of the total responses (25.9% of compliant and 31.6% of deficient profiles). Excluding these artifacts, the model also cited at least one issue other than the designed error in all the compliant profile responses and 59.7% of the deficient profile responses.

Ablation 3: prompt specificity

Given the low correct withholding rates observed for profiles with injected issues or errors, we tested whether targeted prompt augmentation could improve error detection. Specifically, the phrase "carefully review date-related information in the patient record" was appended to the standard prompt used for the main experiment (Supplementary Prompt 6) and evaluated on 125 randomly selected deficient profiles (25 per category) using Gemini 3 Pro as a representative model, which had shown 0% correct withholding in the main experiment.

Since this ablation was conducted within the same time window as the main experiment (Supplementary Table S4), the main-experiment outcomes on the same profiles serve as a concurrent baseline. As shown in Figure 4(d), this prompt modification produced substantial improvements in correct withholding for date-sensitive profiles: profiles with subscriber age error improved to 96.0% correct withholding, and profiles with chronological errors reached 100.0%. However, the benefit was not uniform: profiles with missing specimen collection date, a required field in the PA portal, reached only 36.0% correct withholding, and the improvement did not generalize to non-date-specific issues (0% correct withholding for profiles with irrelevant clinical history and 29.2% for profiles with duplicate patient names).

Manual review of agent outputs on the clinically irrelevant profiles clarified the mechanism: agents consistently halted by citing the specimen collection date as being in the past, reasoning that a pre-authorization cannot be submitted for a procedure that has already taken place. This is a misconception about the PA workflow: the service under authorization is the sequencing test itself, and specimen collection prior to authorization is routine in practice.

Discussion

In this study, we developed a sandbox and evaluation framework for LLM-based browser agents performing ES/GS PA submission, focusing on whether agents halt properly when patient information contains errors. This capability is critical given the prevalence of clinical documentation errors, 19, 20 yet it remains understudied in existing agent benchmarks 15, [21] [22] [23].

Across the three models evaluated, agents rarely withheld submission for the correct reason, reflecting a systematic bias toward form submission that poses operational and compliance risks in PA workflows. The human baseline suggests that the gap between agents and a human reviewer may be narrower for administrative errors, which the genetic counselor also largely missed, than for assessments of clinical appropriateness. Because the baseline comprised a single reviewer on 30 profiles, a larger multi-reviewer study would be needed to establish a formal human-performance benchmark.

The sandbox used in this study simplifies the real PA workflow and EHR environment, as reproducing a production EHR was not feasible within the scope of this study. This simplification can, however, be viewed as a lower bound on task difficulty that sets a minimum standard for agent performance: if an agent cannot reliably identify issues when the information is presented in a structured and searchable format, it is unlikely to perform better Our agent experiment results carry several important implications. First, Ablation 2 suggests that, outside an agentic workflow, the same model scrutinizes inputs broadly and flags anomalies indiscriminately, and that this scrutiny is suppressed to some extent once the model is embedded in a workflow focused on task execution. The error analysis points in the same direction: in clinically irrelevant profiles, agents extracted the clinical narrative but did not evaluate whether it supported testing. However, this pattern cannot be cleanly attributed to a single component, since the non-agent and agent conditions differ on multiple dimensions simultaneously, such as task framing, attentional load, output modality and browser interaction. Second, relaxing the maximum step limit substantially increases task completion rates, while also leading the agent to consume more steps to complete the same tasks under a looser budget. Cost-effectiveness should therefore also be considered in design.

For an example task, the resulting computing cost was approximately $1.72 for Claude Opus 4.5 (30 steps), $0.65 for Gemini 3 Pro (40 steps), and $0.17 for Gemini 3 Flash (30 steps); or roughly $0.057, $0.016, and $0.006 per step, respectively, after accounting for prompt caching. Even though the lighter model needed a larger max step limit to reach completion rates comparable to the frontier models, its overall cost could remain lower. It should be noted that these estimates reflect only the computing cost of individual agent runs in our sandbox and should not be taken to approximate the cost of real-world deployment, which must also account for operational and maintenance costs and the labor cost of human supervision. Characterizing these cost components will be an important consideration for future work.

Third, while augmenting agent prompts with error-specific information improved performance on the targeted error types, the targeted prompt operates narrowly on its intended category rather than conferring general improvements in agent reasoning. Prior work shows that prompt engineering is highly context-and task-dependent, often improving some subtasks while degrading others, and remains sensitive to small variations in phrasing or format. 24 This brittleness makes exhaustive prompt engineering an impractical strategy for clinical deployment, as it would require anticipating every possible failure mode in advance.

In practice, a structured onboarding or "shadowing" phase, during which the agent observes real submission workflows, encounters errors, and iteratively refines its own prompts or skill documents, is likely necessary to achieve broad coverage. 25, 26 Finally, our results suggest that reliable error detection and form submission may be fundamentally difficult to achieve within a single autonomous agent at current model capability. A controlled, modular workflow may be a better architecture for clinical deployment, given that PA submission for ES/GS itself is a coordinated team effort: administrative staff compile patient information from the EHR, a genetic counselor or PA specialist reviews documentation for completeness and clinical appropriateness, and a designated submitter enters the finalized form. 27, 28 A multi-agent pipeline would mirror this workflow naturally, and emerging evidence suggests that multiagent designs outperform monolithic LLM agents in clinical tasks. 29, 30 This staged design can also position a human reviewer as a deliberate participant rather than a final rubber stamp: the agent's output should first be presented to a geneticist in a human-readable format, with each identified issue paired to its supporting evidence, before any submission is triggered.

However, whether such a pipeline delivers net time savings in practice will depend on how human oversight is designed, including at which points the agent pauses for review, when a human intervenes or halts the trajectory, and how much of the output must be verified. These are open human-AI interaction questions that warrant dedicated future work.

Several limitations bound the interpretation of our findings. First, the EHR environment was deliberately simplified and understates the burden of a production EHR: the information required for a single payer's PA form was consolidated into one structured record, whereas in practice some of these fields would not appear directly in clinical documentation. In addition, some generated fields carry artifacts of the synthetic data generation process that do not conform to real-world conventions (e.g., randomly generated NPI numbers and addresses) that introduce noise and make it harder to distinguish genuine reasoning failures from responses to unrealistic data. The use of synthetic data itself, however, was a deliberate design choice rather than solely a constraint: exposing an unvalidated agentic workflow to real patient records would carry privacy and safety risks, and synthetic profiles allow error types to be injected and controlled systematically. Building on our findings, a clinically validated cohort, for example, one drawn from de-identified real PA submissions with clinical reviews to define compliant and deficient cases, will be an important direction for future work. Second, we evaluated agents under a single baseline prompt template and did not systematically test alternative prompting strategies which could meaningfully shift the behaviors we observed. In addition, the agent and non-agent prompts in Ablation 2 were not identically worded because of the difference in setting. The agent prompt instructed the agent to "verify all required fields and then directly submit," framing submission as the default action with halting as the exception, whereas the non-agent prompt asked the model to "determine if the pre-authorization form should be submitted," framing the task as an open decision. Since this difference in framing could bias the agent toward submission, the contrast between the two settings may also partly reflect prompt wording rather than agentic scaffolding itself. Finally, the models evaluated in this study only represent the agent capabilities available at the time of the study. Given the pace of model development, the specific rates we report may not hold for newer models, and the sandbox is intended to support re-evaluation as new models are released rather than serve as a fixed ranking. function that directs to the synthetic EHR database. The payer portal requires authentication prior to form access. The EHR interface supports patient retrieval via name-based search, and each patient record contains structured data fields (demographics, subscriber, provider, laboratory, and test details) alongside a free-text clinical summary. (b) Patient profile generation process. All profiles were generated from predefined clinical condition templates and ICD codes, and subsequently augmented with LLM-generated freetext clinical narratives conditioned on the structured data. (c) A browser-based agent was initialized with a standardized prompt, and a unique task ID was automatically assigned at the time of task creation. Each task was executed in an independent session within the controlled sandbox environment per patient profile and per model, with no shared state or memory across runs. A maximum of 40 browser interaction steps were enforced per task, and the thinking mode was enabled to produce explicit intermediate reasoning traces, including step-level evaluation, short-term memory, and nextaction planning. (d) Task outcomes for all patient profiles are evaluated against ground-truth data. For compliant profiles, submitted forms are assessed for form-level and field-level accuracy; halted submissions are flagged as over-refusal. For deficient profiles, submission is considered undesired, while halted submissions can be either correct withholding or error misattribution depending on whether the identified issue matches the ground-truth injected error. Tasks that terminate without producing either a submission or withholding decision, such as due to step limit exhaustion, data loss, or other technical failures, are classified as aborted. b) breaks down outcomes on deficient profiles by issue type. Both Gemini 3 Flash and Claude Opus 4.5 correctly withheld profiles with a missing collection date (Gemini 3 Flash 32.0%, Claude Opus 4.5 10.0%) or irrelevant clinical history only (Gemini 3 Flash 39.0%, Claude Opus 4.5 17.0%).

Figure 2(d) shows variability at the level of individual tasks: fewer than half of tasks produced identical outcomes across all three runs (Gemini 3 Pro 48.0%, Gemini 3 Flash 22.0%, Claude Opus 4.5 18.0%). Even Exp 2 and Exp 3, conducted together on the same model state, showed frequent task-level flipping (Figure 2(e)), with pairwise agreement of only 58.0% (Gemini 3 Pro), 50.0% (Gemini 3 Flash), and 39.0% (Claude Opus 4.5). Thus, agent outcomes on fixed inputs can be substantially non-deterministic, and stable aggregate percentages do not necessarily imply stable task-level outcomes.

in a real-world setting. The realistic clinical deployment of an agentic PA pipeline would therefore look substantially different from the sandbox. Patient information should be retrieved programmatically from the institution's EHR through a standard interface such as Health Level Seven (HL7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), which exposes structured resources of each individual patient without having to navigate EHR user interfaces. The agent would then interact with the payer portal only for form filling, a step naturally suited to browser-based automation.
